Today marks the 12th anniversary of a vision rooted in the simple belief that "India can manufacture for the world". 🇮🇳

Looking back on 2014, one may recall debates about India's manufacturing potential. At a time when many products used in India were imported, PM Narendra Modi ji refused to accept that as our fate.

He envisioned an India that would not only manufacture for its own needs but would also create products for the world. An India where products used across the globe would proudly carry the tag 'Made in India' and be known for their quality.

We are witnessing that vision taking shape.

The numbers tell an encouraging story. India recorded its highest-ever annual FDI inflow of USD 94.53 billion in FY 2025-26, while cumulative FDI inflows from FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26 reached USD 843 billion.

Greenfield industrial smart cities are being set up across the country under the National Industrial Corridor Development Programme to build infrastructure for globally competitive manufacturing.

Ease of Doing Business reforms have simplified regulations and reduced the compliance burden, while reforms in key sectors have created new opportunities for investment and manufacturing.

The PLI schemes have added further momentum. As of March 31, 2026, they have resulted in ₹2.40 lakh crore of actual investment, ₹23.8 lakh crore in production/sales and ₹15.2 lakh crore in exports, while generating over 14.6 lakh direct & indirect jobs.

Sectors such as electronics and telecom, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, automobiles, IT hardware, and speciality steel have significantly benefited from the PLI schemes.

The Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) is giving a huge boost to small enterprises, and over 470 crore orders have been placed through the platform.

But the real story of Make in India goes beyond these numbers.

It is the confidence it has created. The confidence among our startup founders, entrepreneurs, manufacturers, innovators, exporters and, most importantly, our people that ‘India can make, India can innovate, and India can compete with the world’.

#12YearsOfMakeInIndia is therefore not just a milestone. It reminds us what can happen when a nation believes in its own capabilities and the government powers that belief with sustained reforms and action.

The journey of Make in India continues, with an even bigger ambition: making India a global manufacturing powerhouse, which will also strengthen our Viksit Bharat by 2047 vision.

C-CAMP - supported, Udupi-based startup BlackFrog receives strong support from Hon’ble Minister Jyotiraditya M Scindia for taking life-saving vaccines to hard-to-reach locations in India’s North East, through its innovative cold-chain vaccine carrier technology.

In partnership with C-CAMP, Blackfrog has enabled the delivery of emergency vaccines and critical medical supplies — including insulin, blood products, breast milk and medical specimens — to some of the remotest locations in Assam and Manipur.

Its active cold-chain technology, Emvolio, maintains the required 2–8°C temperature range, preventing temperature-sensitive medicines and vaccines from degrading or losing their efficacy during last-mile transportation — helping ensure life-saving healthcare supplies reach even the hardest-to-reach communities safely and effectively

With C-CAMP’s support, the technology has also been deployed in remote locations across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

C-CAMP has also supported Blackfrog through multiple programmes, including IT BT Department, Karnataka #KSAPBIO50 cohort, Atal Innovation Mission Official #SeedFund cohort, and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) COVID Fund cohort; Blackfrog is also a #NBEC2019 winner.

India’s carbon market is taking shape. Is your startup building for what comes next?

The development of the Indian Carbon Market is creating new infrastructure and mechanisms around how greenhouse gas reductions and removals can be measured, verified and translated into carbon credit certificates. The framework includes both a compliance mechanism and an offset mechanism.

This is creating opportunities for startups building across the carbon ecosystem, from measurement and accounting to carbon removal, crediting, verification and climate finance.

The Climate Incubation Hub, an initiative by Hindustan Unilever Limited in partnership with NSRCEL, is looking for climate-tech startups working on:
• Carbon Capture & Storage
• Carbon Accounting Platforms
• Carbon Offsets
• Carbon Credits
• Climate Finance Enablers

The opportunity is not only in generating carbon credits. It is also in building the technology, data, verification and financial infrastructure needed for credible and scalable carbon markets.

For startups with 1+ year of operations, a market-ready product, existing customers and early revenue, the Climate Incubation Hub offers:

Mentorship | Grants | Investor Access | Ecosystem Access | Product-Market Fit | Cohort-Based Learning | Governance & Strategy

Applications are closing soon.

Ask someone to define a social enterprise, and you will hear a familiar answer. Low profits. Services for the poor. A business with its heart in the right place... 

Then push a little:

Does a low-cost TB vaccine qualify? A device that allows home screening for cervical cancer in rural households? Affordable diagnostic devices? A household-level biodigester? Sodium-ion batteries for energy storage? Green concrete? Soil-microbiome restoration? Effluent treatment that returns clean water to the planet? 

The reflex comes quickly. "That is deep science, not social." 

That reflex is the myth. The deeper error is treating "science" and "social" as competing categories. They answer different questions. Science describes the risk you are taking. Social describes whose problem you have chosen, and whether the market can capture the return. 

So what should earn the word social? Not the legal structure. Not the optics. Not whether the founder has chosen to make a profit. Two questions do the work:

1 - What problem are you solving that the market is not already solving?
2- What risk are you absorbing that conventional enterprise refuses to hold? 

Seen this way, a deep-science venture addressing a neglected disease, climate resilience, clean energy, water security or sustainable materials is every bit as much an act of social entrepreneurship as a last-mile service-delivery organisation. 

The misclassification has consequences. The problem is not semantic. We have built capital systems around categories, and an innovation that does not fit the category becomes orphaned. It is why some of the most consequential technologies society needs struggle to get funded, and why some never get built.

For decades, our most celebrated social enterprises created new models to reach people conventional markets had overlooked. Amul, Aravind Eye Care, SELCO and many others redesigned distribution, financing, access and delivery. That work remains essential.

But the frontier is moving upstream. The hardest problems we now face cannot be solved through distribution innovation alone. Sometimes the missing molecule, material, diagnostic, energy system or production technology simply does not exist. It has to be invented. And once invented, it still has to be tested, validated, financed, deployed, adopted and taken to scale. Which means the social entrepreneur of the future is as likely to emerge from a laboratory, an engineering workshop or a clinical validation site as from a development organisation.

The defining question was never profit versus non-profit. It is whether you are solving problems society urgently needs solved and markets systematically undervalue, and whether you will take the scientific, entrepreneurial and market-creation risks required to solve them. Increasingly, those problems run through deep science. That is not outside social entrepreneurship. It is its next frontier.

B2B or B2C? Your customer decides how you should go to market. 👇

A strong product is only one part of the equation. Your Go-To-Market (GTM) strategy needs to change based on who you're selling to.

In B2B, buying decisions often involve multiple stakeholders, longer evaluation cycles, business value, reliability, and measurable results.

In B2C, the journey is often more direct, with factors such as price, convenience, brand, experience, and customer preference playing a major role.

For startups, understanding this difference can help you make better decisions around:

🔹 Who your real decision-maker is
🔹 What motivates your customer to buy
🔹 Where you should reach them
🔹 How your sales journey should work
🔹 Which metrics actually matter
